stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.fps.xn.justification: The coefficientwise content matches: `PowerSeries.XnEquiv` is `∀ m ≤ n, coeff m f = coeff m g`, exactly the informal definition requiring equality for `m ∈ {0,…,n}`, and `PowerSeries.X ^ (n + 1) ∣ f - g` expresses that `f-g` is a multiple of `x^(n+1)`. However, the elaborated target quantifies `∀ {R : Type u_3} [CommRing R]`, while the blueprint only refers to coefficients in `K` and none of the supplied informal definitions or context specifies what algebraic structure `K` has. Thus it is impossible to determine whether `[CommRing R]` merely encodes the intended setting, is a more general formulation (if `K` was intended to be a field), or is a contentful restriction (if more general coefficient rings were intended). The package would need a declaration fixing `K`—for example, that it is a commutative ring or field—to decide faithfulness.

The elaborated target adds the mathematically contentful binder `[inst : CommRing R]`, whereas the blueprint only says “Let a,b,c,d ∈ K[[x]]” and states no commutative-ring hypothesis on `K`. The composition definition used here involves only zero, addition, multiplication, and finite sums, so additive inverses are not part of this proposition’s stated assumptions. The restriction enters through `PowerSeries.subst`, whose signature itself requires `[CommRing R]`; by contrast, `PowerSeries.XnEquiv` is already defined under `[CommSemiring R]`. To make the formalization faithful, provide/generalize substitution with the informal coefficient formula over a commutative semiring and change the target binder to `[CommSemiring R]` (or explicitly add the commutative-ring assumption to the blueprint). Apart from this restriction, `XnEquiv` exactly expresses equality of coefficients for every `m ≤ n`, the two constant-coefficient hypotheses match `[x^0]c=[x^0]d=0`, and `PowerSeries.subst c a`/`PowerSeries.subst d b` represent the stated compositions.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.gf-ws..justification: The two declarations together express both conclusions of the blueprint. The finite-type part is exactly `W₁.IsFiniteType → W₂.IsFiniteType → (W₁ +ᵥ W₂).IsFiniteType`, matching “Let A and B be two finite-type weighted sets. Then, A+B is finite-type.” Here `IsFiniteType` is definitionally `∀ n : ℕ, {a | W.weight a = n}.Finite`, and `disjointUnion` uses the tagged sum `α ⊕ β` with inherited weights via `Sum.elim W₁.weight W₂.weight`, matching disjoint union. The generating-function part assumes `hft₁ : W₁.IsFiniteType` and `hft₂ : W₂.IsFiniteType` and concludes `(W₁ +ᵥ W₂).weightGenFun ⋯ = W₁.weightGenFun hft₁ + W₂.weightGenFun hft₂`, exactly matching `\overline{A+B}=\overline A+\overline B`. The binder `{R} [CommSemiring R]` makes the identity more general than the blueprint’s integer-coefficient formulation: `weightGenFun` casts each finite cardinality into `R`, and the theorem holds for every such coefficient semiring. This is a stronger conclusion rather than an added restriction on the weighted sets, so it is faithful.

The blueprint assumes “two isomorphic finite-type weighted sets” and concludes “Ā = B̄.” The Lean signature has exactly the corresponding data and hypotheses: `(W₁ : WeightedSet α) (W₂ : WeightedSet β) (hft₁ : W₁.IsFiniteType) (hft₂ : W₂.IsFiniteType), (W₁ ≅ᵥ W₂) → ...`. Here `IsFiniteType` means each weight fiber is finite, and `AreIsomorphic`/`≅ᵥ` means `Nonempty (W₁.Isomorphism W₂)`, where an isomorphism is a weight-preserving equivalence, matching the informal definitions. The conclusion `W₁.weightGenFun hft₁ = W₂.weightGenFun hft₂` is equality of the series whose nth coefficients are the cardinalities of the weight-n fibers. The additional universal choice `{R} [CommSemiring R]` makes the theorem more general than the blueprint’s explicitly integer-valued generating functions: specializing to `R = ℤ` gives the stated result. Thus this is harmless strengthening, not an added restricting hypothesis.

Together the two targets formalize both clauses of the blueprint. `WeightedSet.pow_isFiniteType` has binders `W : WeightedSet α`, `W.IsFiniteType`, and `k : ℕ`, and concludes `(W.pow k).IsFiniteType`, exactly matching “Let A be a finite-type weighted set. Let k ∈ ℕ. Then, A^k is finite-type.” The dependency `WeightedSet.pow` realizes the Cartesian power as functions `Fin k → α`, with weight `∑ i, W.weight (f i)`, which is the standard k-tuple Cartesian power with summed weights required by the informal definitions. `WeightedSet.weightGenFun_pow` assumes the same `hft : W.IsFiniteType` and concludes `(W.pow k).weightGenFun ⋯ = W.weightGenFun hft ^ k`, matching `\overline{A^k}=\overline A^k`; the omitted argument is the finite-type proof supplied by the first result, not an added hypothesis. The formal equality is quantified over every `[CommSemiring R]`, whereas the blueprint defines the generating function over `ℤ`; this is a stronger, more general coefficient-ring conclusion, and specializing to integer coefficients gives the stated result.

The two declarations jointly formalize both conclusions. `WeightedSet.prod_isFiniteType` states `W₁.IsFiniteType → W₂.IsFiniteType → (W₁ ×ᵥ W₂).IsFiniteType`, exactly matching “Then, A×B is finite-type.” The product definition uses the Cartesian type `α × β` and weight `W₁.weight a + W₂.weight b`, matching the informal product definition. `WeightedSet.weightGenFun_prod` assumes `(hft₁ : W₁.IsFiniteType) (hft₂ : W₂.IsFiniteType)` and concludes `(W₁ ×ᵥ W₂).weightGenFun ⋯ = W₁.weightGenFun hft₁ * W₂.weightGenFun hft₂`, matching `\overline{A\times B}=\overline A\cdot\overline B`. Its quantification over every `[CommSemiring R]` is more general than the blueprint’s integer-coefficient FPS and includes the intended coefficient setting, so it strengthens rather than weakens the result. The `[DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]` binders are decidability/implementation instances used to support finite counting, not a mathematical restriction on the weighted sets.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.gf.pro.justification: The blueprint states the FPS identity over a “commutative ring” and its definition imposes no integral-domain condition. The elaborated target instead assumes both `[CommRing K]` and the additional binder `[NoZeroDivisors K]`. By the supplied docstring, this requires `a * b = 0` to imply `a = 0` or `b = 0`, excluding commutative rings with zero divisors, so the Lean theorem is weaker than the blueprint. The topology-related binders can serve to encode `∏'` as a topological infinite product, but `[NoZeroDivisors K]` is a mathematically contentful algebraic restriction unrelated to that encoding. To make the declaration faithful, remove the `[NoZeroDivisors K]` binder and prove the identity for arbitrary `[CommRing K]`, retaining only whatever topology assumptions are genuinely needed to represent the coefficientwise FPS products.

The formal equality matches the blueprint term-for-term: `∏' (i : { n // Odd ↑n }), Ring.inverse (1 - PowerSeries.X ^ ↑↑i)` indexes the left side by odd elements of `ℕ+`, while `∏' (k : ℕ+), (1 + PowerSeries.X ^ ↑k)` indexes the right side by all positive integers. `PowerSeries.X` is the formal variable, and `Ring.inverse` is the total inverse; here each `1 - X^i` is invertible as a formal power series, so it represents the blueprint’s `(1-x^i)⁻¹`. The binders `[TopologicalSpace K] [IsTopologicalRing K] [T2Space K]` encode the setting required by the library’s topology-based `tprod`; for these coefficientwise-stabilizing products this serves as the formal implementation of the blueprint’s infinite product rather than changing its mathematical content. The blueprint’s geometric-series definition assumes `K` is a field, whereas the target only requires `[CommRing K] [NoZeroDivisors K]`; this is algebraically more general, not weaker than the blueprint. Every field satisfies those algebraic assumptions, and a suitable topology (for example, the discrete topology) supplies the encoding instances.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.gf.wei.justification: The target only proves a restricted forward classification: `∀ (n : ℕ) ... T.isFaultfree → n ≥ 1 → (A-case ∨ B-case ∨ C-case)`. First, the binder `n ≥ 1 →` is an added, mathematically contentful hypothesis. The informal statement ranges over “the faultfree domino tilings of height-3 rectangles,” while its rectangle definition allows `R_{n,m}` “for any `n,m ∈ ℕ`”; it does not exclude `n = 0`. Thus the Lean theorem does not imply the stated classification at width zero. Second, “are precisely the tilings” asserts both directions, including that every listed `A_{2k}`, `B_{2k}`, and `C` is faultfree, whereas the target only assumes `T.isFaultfree` and derives membership in the list; it contains no converse faultfreeness assertions. `TilingEquiv` is otherwise an appropriate representation-level replacement for mathematical equality. To make the declaration faithful, remove the target’s `n ≥ 1` restriction (or, if positive width was intended, add that restriction to the blueprint) and formulate an iff/equality-of-classes that also proves the listed tilings are faultfree.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.lgv.1-.justification: The numerical definition `numPaths` is extensionally compatible with the blueprint: although it branches on the stronger-looking condition `a.1 ≤ b.1 ∧ a.2 ≤ b.2`, every remaining case with nondecreasing coordinate sum has blueprint binomial value zero—either the lower argument is not natural, or it exceeds the nonnegative upper argument. Likewise, `no_paths_when_sum_decreases` exactly matches the blueprint’s zero case via `b.coordSum < a.coordSum` and `coordSum p = p.1 + p.2`. However, the declaration connecting the formula to the actual number of paths is `∀ (a b) (hfin : (pathsFromTo a b).Finite), numPaths a b = hfin.toFinset.card`. The binder `hfin` is an added, mathematically contentful finiteness hypothesis absent from “the # of paths from (a,b) to (c,d).” Thus the theorem only proves correctness after finiteness is supplied and does not itself establish that every `pathsFromTo a b` is finite. To be faithful, the project should establish `∀ a b, (pathsFromTo a b).Finite` and state the cardinality theorem using that unconditional finiteness result (or package existence of the finiteness witness together with the cardinality equality), rather than requiring `hfin` from the caller.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.lgv.2p.justification: The target quantifies over exactly the four unrestricted lattice points required by the blueprint: `∀ (A A' B B' : LGV1.LatticePoint)`, with `LatticePoint = ℤ × ℤ`. Its left side is `(pathMatrix2 A A' B B').det`, where `pathMatrix2` has entries `numPaths A B`, `numPaths A B'`, `numPaths A' B`, and `numPaths A' B'`, matching the displayed path-count matrix. `numPaths` gives the binomial count for east/north lattice paths when the endpoint is reachable and zero otherwise. Its right side is `↑(numNipats2 A A' B B') - ↑(numNipats2 A A' B' B)`, exactly the number of nipats from `(A,A')` to `(B,B')` minus those from `(A,A')` to `(B',B)`. The dependency `PathTuple.isNonIntersecting` requires distinct paths to have disjoint vertex sets, matching the informal definition that no two paths share a vertex. The casts to `ℤ` merely place the natural-number counts in the determinant's coefficient ring so subtraction has the intended integer meaning. No additional hypotheses or restricted quantifiers are introduced.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.lgv.jo.justification: The main theorem exactly matches the blueprint. It quantifies over all four lattice points and assumes `LGV1.isWeaklyNorthwestOf A' A` and `LGV1.isWeaklyNorthwestOf B' B`; by the definition `fun p q => p.x ≤ q.x ∧ p.y ≥ q.y`, these are precisely the two displayed northwest coordinate conditions. It then quantifies over arbitrary paths `p p'`, with premises `p.isPathFromTo A B'` and `p'.isPathFromTo A' B`, and concludes `∃ v ∈ p.vertices A, v ∈ p'.vertices A'`, exactly saying that the paths have a common vertex. The path definitions use lists of only `east` and `north` steps, matching the informal integer-lattice digraph, and `vertices` includes the starting point and all subsequently visited points. The corollary `LGV1.numNipats2 A A' B' B = 0` uses source tuple `![A,A']` and target tuple `![B',B]`, exactly the informal `(A,A')` to `(B',B)`. Although `Set.ncard` is zero for infinite sets as well, here paths between fixed endpoints consist of fixed finite numbers of east and north steps, so the relevant path-tuple set is finite; thus cardinality zero expresses that there are no nipats.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.lgv.kp.justification: The elaborated signature quantifies exactly as required: `∀ {k : ℕ} (A B : LGV1.kVertex k)` corresponds to “Let `k ∈ ℕ`” and two `k`-vertices, with no added mathematical hypotheses. By `kVertex k = Fin k → ℤ × ℤ`, these are precisely finite tuples of lattice points. The left side `(LGV1.pathMatrixK A B).det` is the determinant of the integer matrix whose entry `(i,j)` is `↑(LGV1.numPaths (A i) (B j))`; `numPaths` counts east/north lattice paths and returns zero when the endpoint is unreachable. The right side `∑ σ, ↑(Equiv.Perm.sign σ) * ↑(LGV1.numNipatsK A B σ)` ranges over all permutations of `Fin k`, uses the permutation sign, and `numNipatsK A B σ = (nipatsFromTo A (B.permute σ)).ncard`, where `B.permute σ i = B (σ i)`. This matches `∑_{σ ∈ S_k} (-1)^σ · (# of nipats from A to σ(B))`. Finally, `nipatsFromTo` uses `PathTuple.isNonIntersecting`, requiring distinct component paths to have disjoint visited-vertex sets, exactly matching the blueprint’s definition that no two paths share a vertex.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.pars.b.justification: The blueprint fixes `n ∈ ℤ` and includes the negative-index clauses “`p_k(n)=0 whenever n<0`” and “`p(n)=0 whenever n<0`”. It also states the recurrence for every integer `n` whenever `k>0`. But the project dependencies are restricted to naturals: `Nat.Partition.partsCount : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ` and `Nat.Partition.partitionCount : ℕ → ℕ`, so negative arguments cannot even be supplied. Correspondingly, the targets quantify only `n : ℕ`, omit clauses (a) and (h), and `partsCount_recurrence` adds the contentful binder `n > 0`; this is needed only because its expressions use saturating natural subtraction, whereas the blueprint uses integer subtraction and requires no such hypothesis. Thus the supplied declarations cannot express the full proposition, rather than merely proving a different statable version. To make it faithful, add integer-indexed definitions, e.g. `partsCount : ℕ → ℤ → ℕ` and `partitionCount : ℤ → ℕ`, agreeing with `Nat.Partition` counts on nonnegative indices and returning zero on negative indices; then state (a)–(h), with recurrence quantified over `n : ℤ` and no `n > 0` assumption. The natural-only targets for (f) and (g) are compatible with those particular clauses, but they do not remedy the package-level mismatch.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.pars.p.justification: The target quantifies exactly as the blueprint does: `∀ (n k : ℕ)`. Its left side is `Nat.Partition.partsCount k n`, whose body is `{p | p.parts.card = k}.card`, exactly the number `p_k(n)` of partitions of `n` into `k` parts. Its right side is `{p | p.largestPart = k}.card`; over the finite type `n.Partition`, this is the number of partitions of `n` whose largest part is `k`. The dependency `largestPart` is `Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, matching the intended largest part, including the empty partition convention. Thus the formal equality states precisely the informal proposition, with no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.pars.q.justification: The blueprint assumes “Let n,k∈ℕ satisfy k>n” and concludes “(n choose k)_q=0.” The Lean binders match this as `(n k : ℕ), n < k → ...`, since `n < k` is exactly `k > n`. By the body of `AlgebraicCombinatorics.qBinomial`, when `n < k` the condition `k ≤ n` is false, so the definition takes its `else 0` branch. The conclusion therefore agrees exactly in the relevant range. The additional binders `∀ {R : Type u_1} [CommSemiring R] ... ∀ (q : R)` make the result more general: it proves the corresponding evaluated identity for every element of every commutative semiring, hence in particular the polynomial/ring instance intended by the blueprint. Requiring only `CommSemiring` rather than the blueprint’s commutative-ring setting is a weaker hypothesis, not drift.

The blueprint quantifies “Let n∈ℕ and k∈ℤ” and explicitly requires the negative-index case: “If k<0, then this is also an empty sum.” Both targets instead bind `(n k : ℕ)`, and the dependency `AlgebraicCombinatorics.qBinomial` itself has type `ℕ → ℕ → R → R`. Thus negative integer values of `k` cannot even be supplied to the project’s q-binomial definition. In addition, target (a) assumes `k ≤ n`, whereas the blueprint also asserts the empty-sum case `k > n`; this restriction enters at the binder `k ≤ n →`. The existing tuple expression cannot simply be used outside that range, since natural subtraction makes `n - k = 0`, and `monotoneFunctions k 0` is not an empty indexing set. To make the proposition faithful, `qBinomial` (or a project-level integer-indexed wrapper) must accept `k : ℤ`, return zero for `k < 0` and `k > n`, and use the tuple sum in range. Then both targets should quantify `k : ℤ`; target (a) should cover all cases with an explicitly empty/zero right-hand side out of range, and target (c) should use the blueprint’s integer-indexed ordinary binomial, also zero for negative `k`.

The blueprint quantifies “For positive integers k and ℓ,” and the elaborated signature has exactly `∀ (k ℓ : ℕ), k ≥ 1 → ℓ ≥ 1 → ...`. Its left-hand side unfolds to `∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc k (k * ℓ), Nat.Partition.partsAndLargestCount k ℓ n`, matching the informal definition `Q(k,ℓ) := ∑_{n=k}^{kℓ} q_{k,ℓ}(n)`. The summand counts partitions satisfying `p.numParts = k ∧ p.largestPart = ℓ`; `numParts` is the cardinality of the parts multiset, and `largestPart` folds `max` from `0`, matching the partition-length condition and the stated empty-partition convention. The right-hand side `(k + ℓ - 2).choose (k - 1)` matches `\binom{k+ℓ-2}{k-1}`. Under `k ≥ 1` and `ℓ ≥ 1`, natural-number subtraction gives the intended nonnegative integer arguments, and `Nat.choose` has the standard binomial-coefficient meaning. No mathematically contentful extra hypothesis or restricted quantifier is introduced.

The binders `∀ (k ℓ : ℕ), 0 < k → 0 < ℓ →` exactly match “for any positive integers k and ℓ.” By the body of `monotoneFunctions`, the left side counts monotone maps `Fin (k - 1) → Fin ((ℓ - 1) + 1)`, i.e. weakly increasing `(k-1)`-tuples with entries in `{0,…,ℓ-1}`. These correspond bijectively to partitions with exactly `k` positive parts and largest part exactly `ℓ`: fix the first (largest) part as `ℓ`, reverse the remaining `k-1` weakly decreasing parts, and subtract `1`. Conversely, reverse this operation and prepend `ℓ`. Thus `(monotoneFunctions (k - 1) (ℓ - 1)).card` is precisely the informal “# of partitions with k parts and largest part ℓ.” Under the positivity hypotheses, the natural-number expression `(k + ℓ - 2).choose (k - 1)` agrees with the informal binomial coefficient `\binom{k+ℓ-2}{k-1}`.

The formal conclusion states only `Tendsto ... (nhds (∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (1 - PowerSeries.X ^ (i + 1))⁻¹))`, corresponding to the endpoint equality with `∏_{i=1}^{k} 1/(1-q^i)`. The blueprint additionally asserts the substantive middle equality `= ∑_{n∈ℕ} (p₀(n)+⋯+pₖ(n)) qⁿ`. No project dependency defines partitions or the functions `p_i(n)`, so that part of the blueprint cannot be expressed using the available formal definitions; the docstring’s mention of partition counts does not add a proposition to the theorem signature. The product indexing itself is correct: `i ∈ Finset.range k` with exponent `i + 1` represents indices `1,…,k`. To make the blueprint statable and the theorem faithful, the project must first define the number of partitions of `n` into exactly `i` parts and the associated power series, then the target must assert both its equality with the limit and its equality with the displayed finite product.

The two declarations exactly cover the two conjuncts of “We have \(\binom n0_q=\binom nn_q=1\) for each \(n\in\mathbb N\).” Their binders quantify over every natural number and every parameter: `∀ {R} [CommSemiring R] (n : ℕ) (q : R)`, with conclusions `qBinomial n 0 q = 1` and `qBinomial n n q = 1`. The project definition uses monotone tuples rather than the blueprint’s partition sum, but at these indices it has exactly one tuple with exponent zero: for `k = 0`, the domain `Fin 0` is empty; for `k = n`, the codomain is `Fin ((n - n) + 1) = Fin 1`. Thus both definitions give `1`. The formal use of `CommSemiring R` is strictly more general than the blueprint’s commutative-ring setting, not an added restriction, and the endpoint indices `0` and `n` are natural numbers despite the blueprint defining the general lower index over integers.

The blueprint quantifies without restriction: “Let $n,k\in\mathbb N$. Then $\binom nk_q=\binom n{n-k}_q$.” The Lean target instead has the added binder `k ≤ n →`, so it proves the identity only on a narrowed range. This restriction is mathematically substantive, not merely encoding. It is necessitated by the dependency `qBinomial : ℕ → ℕ → R → R` together with natural-number saturated subtraction: when `k > n`, `n - k = 0`, while the body makes `qBinomial n k q = 0` but generally makes `qBinomial n 0 q = 1`. By contrast, the informal q-binomial definition allows an integer lower index, so for `k > n` the complementary index `n-k` is negative rather than zero. To be faithful, remove the `k ≤ n` binder and change the dependency to support integer lower indices (with out-of-range coefficients zero), or formulate the complementary side with an explicit out-of-range-zero guard. The generalization from a commutative ring/polynomial identity to evaluation in any `CommSemiring R` is stronger and is not itself drift.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.perm.c.justification: The target quantifies over exactly the finite permutation setting: `∀ {α : Type u_1} [Fintype α] (f : Equiv.Perm α) (i j : α)`. Its conclusion `f.SameCycle i j ↔ ∃ p, (f ^ p) i = j` is the blueprint’s third condition, since equality symmetry identifies `(f ^ p) i = j` with `j = σ^p(i)`, and `p` is a natural number via `Equiv.Perm.instPowNat`. The omitted-looking middle condition follows by instantiating the universally quantified theorem with `j` and `i` exchanged: `SameCycle` is documented as an equivalence relation, hence symmetric, and `(f ^ p) j = i` is equivalent to `i = (f ^ p) j`. Thus the single universally quantified iff implies the entire displayed chain of equivalences.

The target quantifies over exactly the intended data, `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n))`, matching “Let `n∈ℕ`. Let `σ∈S_n`,” since `Fin n` is a canonical `n`-element set and `Equiv.Perm` is its symmetric group. Its conclusion `Equiv.Perm.sign σ = (-1) ^ (n - ...numCyclesTotal σ)` matches `(-1)^σ = (-1)^(n-k)`: the library sign is the permutation parity (`1` for even and `-1` for odd), while `numCyclesTotal` has body `σ.cycleFactorsFinset.card + (Fintype.card α - σ.support.card)`, counting the nontrivial disjoint cycles plus the fixed points, hence exactly the cycles “including the 1-cycles.” Replacing the informally introduced `k` satisfying that count by this canonical count is equivalent, not a restriction. The use of `Fin n` rather than `[n]={1,…,n}` and of integer units `ℤˣ` rather than integers is representational encoding; both sides are signs ±1, so the equality carries the same mathematical content.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.perm.l.justification: The formal declaration quantifies over exactly `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n))` and asserts `invCount σ = ∑ i, lehmerEntry σ i`; by the dependency bodies, this equates the number of pairs `i < j ∧ σ i > σ j` with the sum over all `i : Fin n` of the corresponding counts. This matches the displayed shape of the blueprint, `ℓ(σ)=ℓ₁(σ)+⋯+ℓₙ(σ)`, and `invCount` is supported by the supplied informal definition of length. However, the package contains no INFORMAL DEFINITION of the blueprint notation `ℓ_i(σ)`—in particular, the referenced `def.perm.lehmer1` is absent. The project definition and docstring for `lehmerEntry` determine the formal side but cannot decide the meaning of the blueprint notation. The omitted informal Lehmer-entry definition is needed to verify that `ℓ_i(σ)` means the number of `j>i` with `σ(i)>σ(j)` (up to the standard order-preserving encoding of `[n]` by `Fin n`).

The target quantifies over exactly two permutations of an n-element ordered set, `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ τ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n))`, and assumes lexicographic comparison of their one-line values: `lexLt (fun i => ↑↑(σ i)) (fun i => ↑↑(τ i))`. By the body of `lexLt`, this means `∃ k, (∀ i < k, a i = b i) ∧ a k < b k`, which is equivalent to the informal definition that the smallest differing coordinate has the smaller entry. Its conclusion applies the same relation to `lehmerEntry σ` and `lehmerEntry τ`. The dependency body `lehmerEntry σ i := {j | i < j ∧ σ i > σ j}.card` exactly matches the informal definition of `ℓ_i(σ)` as the number of later positions carrying smaller values. The use of zero-based `Fin n` rather than `[n] = {1,…,n}` is only an order-preserving reindexing of the same n positions and values, so it does not change lexicographic order or Lehmer entries. The casts to `ℤ` merely place the natural-valued coordinates in the integer tuples required by `lexLt`. There are no added mathematical hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

The target quantifies over two integer n-tuples as functions, `∀ {n : ℕ} (a b : Fin n → ℤ)`, assumes exactly that they are distinct, `a ≠ b`, and concludes the required disjunction, `lexLt a b ∨ lexLt b a`. The dependency defines `lexLt a b` as `∃ k, (∀ i < k, a i = b i) ∧ a k < b k`: all earlier coordinates agree, while the first differing coordinate satisfies `a k < b k`. This is equivalent to the informal definition using the smallest `k ∈ [n]` with `a_k ≠ b_k`. Representing the coordinates `1,…,n` by the zero-based type `Fin n` is an indexing encoding and does not change the mathematical claim.

The blueprint quantifies over “Let n ∈ ℕ and σ ∈ S_n” and concludes “ℓ(σ⁻¹) = ℓ(σ).” The elaborated signature quantifies over exactly the corresponding data, “∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)), σ⁻¹.length = σ.length,” with no added hypotheses. By `Equiv.Perm.length`, length is `σ.inversions.card`, and `Equiv.Perm.inversions` consists of pairs satisfying `p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.2 < σ p.1`, exactly the informal condition i < j and σ(i) > σ(j). `Fin n` uses the order-isomorphic zero-based model of the informal set `[n] = {1,…,n}`; shifting indices by one preserves order, inversions, and inverse permutations. Thus the formal equality is the stated equality of Coxeter lengths.

The binder `∀ (n x : ℕ)` makes `x` a natural number, so `x ^ invCount σ`, all sums, and all products are computed in `ℕ`. In the blueprint, however, `x` is the polynomial/FPS indeterminate: `def.fps.x` says “Let x denote the FPS (0,1,0,0,...)”, and the claimed equality is the generating-polynomial identity ending in `[n]_x! ∈ ℤ[x]`. Thus the target states the identity only after evaluation at natural-number values of `x`, rather than as an equality of polynomials/formal power series. The permutation indexing and product bounds are otherwise equivalent: `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` models `S_n`, and `i ∈ range n` with `j ∈ range (i+1)` gives the factors `[1]_x⋯[n]_x`, with the extra `i=0` factor equal to 1. To be faithful, change the target’s `x : ℕ` binder and ambient arithmetic to the polynomial/FPS setting with `x` the indeterminate; alternatively, state a sufficiently general identity over a commutative ring/semiring and then specialize it to the polynomial indeterminate.

The blueprint fixes “Let n ∈ ℕ” and, in part (f), “For any k ∈ ℤ”; the elaborated binders are exactly `∀ {n : ℕ} (k : ℤ)`. Its `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` represents permutations of an ordered n-element set, matching `σ ∈ S_n`. By the dependency bodies, `invCount σ = (inv σ).card` and `inv σ = {p | p.1 < p.2 ∧ σ p.1 > σ p.2}`, exactly the blueprint’s definition of ℓ(σ) as the number of inversions. The conclusion compares the cardinalities satisfying `↑(invCount σ) = k` and `↑(invCount σ) = ↑(n.choose 2) - k`, matching the two counts with lengths `k` and `binom n 2 - k`. The casts to ℤ correctly permit every integer k, including values outside the possible natural length range, and `Nat.choose n 2` agrees with the blueprint binomial coefficient for `n ∈ ℕ` and lower argument 2.

Both targets use the crucial term `σ * Equiv.swap i j`, while the blueprint fixes multiplication explicitly: “we will write `α β` for the composition `α ∘ β`,” so `σ t_{i,j}` must act as `σ ∘ t_{i,j}`. The package gives only `Equiv.Perm.instMul : Mul (Equiv.Perm α)` and the generic statement that the meaning of `*` is type-dependent; it does not provide the instance body or a permutation-specific multiplication docstring. Hence it is impossible from the package to determine whether `σ * Equiv.swap i j` means `σ ∘ swap i j` or the opposite composition. This affects both `length_mul_transposition` and `length_mul_transposition_compare`, not merely notation. If the instance implements `(σ * τ)(x) = σ(τ(x))`, the declarations faithfully encode parts (b) and (a), respectively; if it implements `(σ * τ)(x) = τ(σ(x))`, they drift, and the product would need to be reversed to `Equiv.swap i j * σ`. The package needs the body or a composition-orientation theorem/docstring for `Equiv.Perm.instMul` to decide.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.perm.r.justification: The target quantifies exactly over the intended data, `∀ {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n))`, matching “Let `n ∈ ℕ` and `σ ∈ S_n`” under the stated `Fin n` convention, with no added hypotheses. Its conclusion, `Equiv.Perm.wordProd σ.canonicalReducedWord = σ`, is the blueprint’s “the product of the canonical reduced word equals σ”; it is equivalent by symmetry of equality to the displayed `σ = a₀ a₁ ⋯ aₙ₋₁`. The dependency bodies preserve the intended construction: `canonicalReducedWord` flattens `lehmerBlock σ` over `List.finRange n` in ascending order, each block lists the indices `i + lehmerEntry σ i - 1, …, i`, `lehmerEntry` counts precisely the `j > i` with `σ i > σ j`, and `wordProd` multiplies the corresponding simple transpositions in list order. Thus the formal declaration faithfully states the blueprint proposition.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.perm.s.justification: The existential theorem alone is weaker than the blueprint: `∀ ... (f : X ≃ Y), Nonempty (Equiv.Perm X ≃* Equiv.Perm Y)` only asserts that some multiplicative equivalence exists, whereas the blueprint specifically asserts that `S_f`, given by `σ ↦ f ∘ σ ∘ f⁻¹`, is a group isomorphism. The companion definition has the appropriately strong result type, `{X} → {Y} → X ≃ Y → Equiv.Perm X ≃* Equiv.Perm Y`, but its body is `fun ... f => f.permCongrHom`. The supplied reference for `Equiv.permCongrHom` says only that it gives an equivalence between the permutation groups; it does not specify that its underlying map sends `σ` to `f ∘ σ ∘ f⁻¹`. Thus the package does not determine whether this definition captures the blueprint’s specified conjugation map. The body or a characterization theorem for `Equiv.permCongrHom` showing its action on each `σ` is needed. If it is conjugation, the companion definition makes the formalization faithful (and the `Nonempty` theorem is merely a weaker corollary); otherwise the definition must be changed to construct the conjugation isomorphism explicitly.

The three declarations exactly encode the three relations, up to the documented zero-based representation of the textbook sets. For (a), `∀ {n : ℕ} (i : Fin (n - 1)), simpleTransposition i * simpleTransposition i = 1` matches “`s_i^2 = id` for all `i ∈ [n-1]`”; in the permutation group, `1` is the identity. For (b), the binders `i j : Fin (n - 1)` give the required index range, and `↑i + 1 < ↑j ∨ ↑j + 1 < ↑i` is equivalent over naturals to `|i-j| > 1`, yielding exactly the stated commutation equality. For (c), `i : Fin (n - 2)` and the locally constructed indices with values `↑i` and `↑i + 1` give precisely `s_i s_{i+1} s_i = s_{i+1} s_i s_{i+1}`. The project definitions `Sn n := Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` and `simpleTransposition i := Equiv.swap ⟨↑i,…⟩ ⟨↑i+1,…⟩` implement the textbook objects after shifting `[n]={1,…,n}` to `Fin n={0,…,n-1}`. Saturating natural subtraction only makes the relevant `Fin` index types empty in the same small-`n` cases where the textbook index sets are empty.

The declarations jointly imply all eight parts. Parts (a), (b), (d), (e), and (f) directly match respectively `sign 1 = 1`, `x ≠ y → sign (swap x y) = -1`, `sign (σ * τ) = sign σ * sign τ`, `sign l.prod = (l.map sign).prod`, and `sign σ⁻¹ = sign σ`. Their binders `{α} [DecidableEq α] [Fintype α]` are more general than the blueprint’s `S_n`; `DecidableEq` is computational encoding, and every `Fin n` supplies both instances. For (c), `σ.IsCycle → sign σ = -(-1) ^ σ.support.card` gives `(-1)^(k-1)` for every nontrivial k-cycle because `-(-1)^k = (-1)^(k-1)`; the blueprint’s exceptional positive case `k = 1`, whose cycle is the identity, is covered jointly by `sign_id`. Part (g), `∏ i, ∏ j ∈ Finset.Ioi i, if σ i < σ j then 1 else -1`, is the stated equivalent inversion-indicator form of the ratio product: each non-inversion contributes `1` and each inversion `-1`. Using `Fin n` rather than `[n]` merely shifts indices from `1,…,n` to `0,…,n-1`. Part (h) exactly quantifies `(R : Type) [CommRing R]`, `σ : Perm (Fin n)`, and `x : Fin n → R`, and its nested `Ioi` products are precisely over `i < j`; the coercion `↑↑(sign σ)` represents the integer sign as an element of `R`. The base-library `Equiv.Perm.sign` is documented as parity, `1` for even and `-1` for odd, agreeing with the informal inversion-parity definition.

The conjugation theorem faithfully strengthens part (a): its binders `(σ : Equiv.Perm α) (e : α ≃ β)` and expression `((e.symm.trans σ).trans e)` denote, from the supplied `Equiv.trans`/`Equiv.symm` documentation, the transported permutation `e ∘ σ ∘ e⁻¹`. Taking `e = φ₁` and `e = φ₂` gives the stated independence from the bijection, and allowing arbitrary finite `β` is more general. However, parts (b) and (c) cannot be fully compared because the package gives only the signatures, not the meanings, of `Equiv.Perm.instOne` and `Equiv.Perm.instMul`. Thus it does not establish that the formal `1` in `Equiv.Perm.sign 1 = 1` is the identity map, or that `σ * τ` in `Equiv.Perm.sign (σ * τ) = ...` is the blueprint product `σ ∘ τ`, which the informal definition explicitly says sends `x` to `σ (τ x)`. The generic `HMul.hMul` documentation even says multiplication is type-dependent. The package would need the instance bodies or facts such as `(1 : Equiv.Perm α) x = x` and `(σ * τ) x = σ (τ x)`. With those standard meanings, all three targets are faithful; the `DecidableEq` binders merely encode what is needed to define the finite-type sign rather than a mathematically substantive restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.sf.e-h.justification: All three declarations imply the corresponding parts of the blueprint. The binders `∀ {K : Type u_1} [CommRing K] {N : ℕ}` match the fixed commutative ring `K` and natural number `N`; quantifying over them is more general than fixing them. In (a), the formal right side `∑ n ∈ Finset.range (N + 1), ... C (e n)` is equivalent to the blueprint’s `∑_{n ∈ ℕ} (-1)^n t^n e_n`, because `e n` is `MvPolynomial.esymm (Fin N) K n`, documented as the sum of degree-`n` squarefree monomials, and hence vanishes for `n > N`. In (b), the outer `MvPolynomial.X 0` and `MvPolynomial.X 1` represent `u` and `v`, while `MvPolynomial.C (MvPolynomial.X i)` embeds the variables of `𝒫`; the range `Finset.range (N + 1)` is exactly `n = 0,…,N`. In (c), `PowerSeries.mk fun n => h n` is the series `∑_{n∈ℕ} t^n h_n`, `↑E` is the polynomial product embedded into the FPS ring, and `(PowerSeries.mk ...) * ↑E = 1` says that this series is the inverse of `E = ∏ᵢ(1-txᵢ)`, which is equivalent in the commutative FPS ring to the displayed product of reciprocals. The extra `[DecidableEq (Fin N)]` binders in (a) and (c) are computational encoding rather than a mathematical restriction: every finite index type `Fin N` has decidable equality, and `h`/`MvPolynomial.hsymm` requires that instance to construct its finite monomial sum.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.sf.ehp.justification: Parts (a) and (b) match the blueprint: `(n : ℕ) (hn : n ≤ N)` formalizes `n ∈ {0,…,N}`, and `∑ mu ∈ NPartitionsOfSize n, monomialSymm mu` uses the supplied size-filtered set of all N-partitions. The use of `[CommSemiring R]` rather than a commutative ring is a valid generalization, while `[DecidableEq (Fin N)]` is computational encoding. However, part (c) adds the binder `n ≠ 0` before `∀ (hN : 0 < N)`, whereas the blueprint says, under `N > 0`, “For each n ∈ ℕ.” This excludes `n = 0` and therefore weakens the theorem. The mismatch originates in the use of `MvPolynomial.psum`: its docstring defines it as “the sum over all the n-th powers of the variables,” so at `n = 0` it gives the constant `N`, while the informal definition explicitly sets `p_0 = 1`; `monomialSymm (singletonPartition 0 hN)` is also `1`. Thus simply deleting `n ≠ 0` would generally make the formal statement false. To be faithful, define a project-level power sum matching the blueprint, with value `1` at zero and `MvPolynomial.psum` for positive degrees, use that on the left-hand side, and remove the `n ≠ 0` binder.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.sf.en-.justification: The blueprint fixes “a commutative ring K” and “an N ∈ ℕ” and states: “For each integer n > N, we have e_n = 0.” The elaborated signature quantifies `∀ {K : Type u_1} [CommRing K] {N n : ℕ}, N < n → ...e n = 0`, and `e` is exactly `MvPolynomial.esymm (Fin N) K n`, whose docstring identifies it as the sum of degree-`n` squarefree monomials. Although Lean takes `n : ℕ` rather than `n : ℤ`, this does not lose any relevant case: since `N ∈ ℕ`, every integer satisfying `n > N` is nonnegative and therefore corresponds to a natural number. Universal quantification over `K` and `N`, rather than keeping arbitrary choices fixed, is the standard equivalent strengthening of the chapter’s fixed-parameter formulation.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.sf.npa.justification: The blueprint states a bijection from “partitions of length ≤ N” to “N-partitions,” given by padding with zeros. The target universally quantifies both parameters, `{N : ℕ} → (n : ℕ) →`, and gives the fiberwise equivalence `{ p // p.parts.card ≤ N } ≃ { mu // NPartition.size mu = n }`, where `p : n.Partition`. Thus, for every size `n`, it bijects partitions of size `n` and length at most `N` with N-partitions of size `n`. Taking all sizes yields the blueprint’s unrestricted bijection, and the formal statement additionally records preservation of size. Its forward map is exactly `NPartition.ofPartition p hp`, whose body pads the descending parts with zeros, while the inverse `mu.toPartition` removes zeros. There are no added mathematical hypotheses.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.sf.sig.justification: The formal binders `sigma : Equiv.Perm (Fin N)`, `f : MvPolynomial (Fin N) R`, and `a : Fin N → ℕ` faithfully encode respectively `σ ∈ S_N`, `f ∈ K[x₁,…,x_N]`, and `(a₁,…,a_N) ∈ ℕ^N`; using `Fin N` instead of `[N]` is only a zero-based finite-index encoding. By the docstring, `MvPolynomial.rename ⇑sigma` renames each variable indexed by `i` to that indexed by `σ(i)`, matching the definition `σ · f = f[x_{σ(1)},…,x_{σ(N)}]`. The right-hand exponent function is exactly `a ∘ ⇑sigma`, whose value at `i` is `a_{σ(i)}`, so the displayed coefficient equality matches the blueprint formula. Although the blueprint fixes a commutative ring `K`, the formal theorem assumes only `[CommSemiring R]`; this is a weaker hypothesis and hence a strictly more general statement that includes the blueprint’s ring case, not drift.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.sf.sn-.justification: The informal statement fixes multiplication in the symmetric group as composition: “we will write αβ for the composition α ∘ β,” and fixes the neutral element as “the identity map id_X.” The targets instead use the base-library operations `1 : Equiv.Perm (Fin N)` and `σ * τ`, via binders `σ τ : Equiv.Perm (Fin N)`, but the supplied references for `Equiv.Perm.instOne` and `Equiv.Perm.instMul` provide only their signatures, with no bodies or docstrings specifying that `1` is the identity bijection and that `(σ * τ) i = σ (τ i)` rather than the opposite composition convention. This is decisive for both `permAction_id` and especially `permAction_mul`. The use of `Fin N` instead of `[N] = {1,…,N}` is merely an equivalent encoding of an N-element indexing set. To determine faithfulness, the package would need the bodies or semantic docstrings of `Equiv.Perm.instOne` and `Equiv.Perm.instMul` establishing their identity and composition conventions.

Together the two declarations formalize both parts of the blueprint. `permAutomorphism` has binders `{K : Type u_1} → [CommRing K] → {N : ℕ} → Equiv.Perm (Fin N) → P K N ≃ₐ[K] P K N`, so for every `σ ∈ S_N` it supplies exactly the claimed “`K`-algebra automorphism of `𝒫`.” Its body is `MvPolynomial.renameEquiv K σ`, with `P K N` defined as `MvPolynomial (Fin N) K`. The use of `Fin N` and `Equiv.Perm (Fin N)` is explicitly licensed by `conv-2eb59533`. Moreover, `permAutomorphismHom` has type `Equiv.Perm (Fin N) →* (P K N ≃ₐ[K] P K N)`, which expresses the first sentence, “The group `S_N` acts on `𝒫` by `K`-algebra automorphisms,” including compatibility with identity and multiplication. The dependency equation `permAutomorphism (σ * τ) = permAutomorphism σ * permAutomorphism τ` agrees with the stated composition convention that `σ * τ` sends `x` to `σ (τ x)`. No mathematically substantive extra hypothesis is added: `[CommRing K]` matches the supplied definition of the coefficient ring.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-prop.sf.str.justification: Both declarations restrict the proposition to already-contained pairs through the binder `(s : SymmetricFunctions.SkewPartition N)`. The restriction enters in `SymmetricFunctions.SkewPartition.mk ... → inner ≤ outer → SkewPartition N`, where `inner ≤ outer` means `∀ i, inner.parts i ≤ outer.parts i`. By contrast, the blueprint begins with arbitrary “two N-partitions” and defines every pair `(μ, λ)` to be a skew partition; containment is part of being a horizontal or vertical strip, not a prerequisite for quantification. Thus the formal declarations omit all non-contained pairs and are weaker than the blueprint. On the restricted domain, the entry conditions are correct: vertical containment supplies `μᵢ ≤ λᵢ`, while `isVerticalStrip` supplies `λᵢ ≤ μᵢ+1`; horizontally, bundled containment supplies every `λᵢ ≥ μᵢ` (including the final one), and `isHorizontalStrip` supplies `μᵢ ≥ λᵢ₊₁`. To make both statements faithful, quantify arbitrary `(outer inner : NPartition N)` and use unbundled strip predicates that themselves include `inner ≤ outer`; alternatively, redefine `SkewPartition` as an unrestricted pair and put containment into `isHorizontalStrip` and `isVerticalStrip`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.accepta.justification: The binders `∀ (n m : ℕ), 0 < n → ∀ I ∈ acceptableSets n m` exactly match “Let n ≥ 1, m ∈ ℕ, and let I be an acceptable set,” since for naturals `0 < n` is equivalent to `n ≥ 1`. The body of `acceptableSets`, `{I ∈ (Finset.range n).powerset | I.card ≤ m}`, expresses precisely `I ⊆ {0,…,n−1}` with `|I| ≤ m`. The conclusion `partner I ∉ acceptableSets n m ↔ 0 ∉ I ∧ I.card = m` exactly matches “the partner I′ is non-acceptable iff 0 ∉ I and |I| = m,” and `partner I := symmDiff I {0}` agrees with the informal definition.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.binom.s.justification: The blueprint quantifies “Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and $k\in\mathbb R$” and its definition assigns a value to $\binom nk$ for arbitrary lower arguments, namely `0` when `k` is not natural. The target instead has binders `∀ {n k : ℕ}, k ≤ n → ...`, so it both restricts `k` to naturals and adds `k ≤ n`. More fundamentally, the only supplied binomial operation is `Nat.choose : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`; it cannot even form the blueprint’s $\binom nk$ for `k : ℝ`, nor implement the stated zero-outside-ℕ definition. Thus the intended statement is not expressible using the available project/base definitions. To make it statable and faithful, the dependencies would need a binomial definition accepting real (or otherwise arbitrary) lower arguments and agreeing with the informal piecewise definition; the theorem should then quantify over all `k : ℝ` without the `k ≤ n` hypothesis.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.binom.u.justification: The blueprint quantifies “Let n ∈ ℂ and k ∈ ℤ,” with its binomial definition explicitly assigning 0 when k ∉ ℕ. By contrast, `binomUpperNegation_int` has binders `∀ (n : ℤ) (k : ℕ)`, narrowing both `n` from complex numbers to integers and `k` from all integers to naturals. Thus it does not cover complex nonintegral `n` or negative `k`. The generic declaration improves the upper argument to `∀ {R} [CommRing R] [BinomialRing R] [NatPowAssoc R] (r : R)`, but still restricts the lower index to `(k : ℕ)` because `Ring.choose` itself has signature `R → ℕ → R`; it therefore also omits the blueprint’s negative-integer cases. To be faithful, the relevant declaration should quantify `n : ℂ` and `k : ℤ` and use an integer-indexed binomial extension that equals `Ring.choose n k.toNat` for nonnegative `k` and `0` for negative `k` (or separately prove the natural and negative cases). The integer specialization alone cannot formalize the stated complex theorem.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.binom.v.justification: The blueprint quantifies over “a,b∈ℂ” and “n∈ℕ” and asserts `binom (a+b) n = ∑_{k=0}^n binom a k binom b (n-k)`. The Lean theorem quantifies more generally over `∀ {S : Type u_2} [CommRing S] [BinomialRing S] (a b : S) (n : ℕ)`, which is a genuine generalization rather than a weakening; its stated setting includes ℂ. `Ring.choose` is documented as the binomial coefficient “interpreted in terms of choosing without replacement,” matching the blueprint’s falling-factorial definition. Finally, `∑ ij ∈ Finset.antidiagonal n, ... ij.1 ... ij.2` ranges over exactly the natural-number pairs `(k,j)` satisfying `k+j=n`; equivalently these are `(k,n-k)` for `0≤k≤n`. Thus the formal right-hand side is precisely the stated convolution sum.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.cancel..justification: The target quantifies exactly as required: `∀ (n d : ℕ)`. By `allEvenTuples n d = Finset.filter IsAllEven Finset.univ`, its cardinal counts functions `Fin n → Fin d`, the finite-type counterpart of tuples in `[d]^n`. The predicate `IsAllEven x = ∀ (k : Fin d), Even {i | x i = k}.card` exactly matches the informal condition that every value occurs an even number of times. The equality `↑(allEvenTuples n d).card * 2 ^ d = ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (d + 1), ↑(d.choose k) * (↑d - 2 * ↑k) ^ n` is an equality in `ℤ`, so `(d-2k)^n` uses signed integer subtraction rather than truncated natural subtraction. `Finset.range (d + 1)` indexes precisely `k = 0,…,d`, and `Nat.choose d k` agrees with the stated binomial coefficient for these natural arguments. Thus the formal equality is exactly the informal division-free formula.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.catalan.justification: The target defines `C := PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(AlgebraicCombinatorics.FPS.catalan n)` and concludes exactly `C = 1 + PowerSeries.X * C ^ 2`, matching the blueprint’s generating function `C(x) = ∑_{n≥0} c_n x^n` and equation `C(x) = 1 + x C(x)^2`. By the dependency body, `catalan n = (2 * n).choose n / (n + 1)` in `ℕ`; this agrees with the informal `c_n = 1/(n+1) * binom(2n,n)` because the relevant binomial coefficient is divisible by `n+1`, after which the result is cast into `ℚ`. `PowerSeries.mk` realizes the coefficient sequence, and `PowerSeries.X` is the formal-series variable. There are no added hypotheses or restricted index binders.

The target states exactly the formal-power-series identity over ℚ: `2 • ((PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(AlgebraicCombinatorics.FPS.catalan n)) * PowerSeries.X) = 1 - PowerSeries.mk fun n => Ring.choose (1 / 2) n * (-4) ^ n`. Here `PowerSeries.mk fun n => ↑(catalan n)` is `C(x)`, `PowerSeries.X` is `x`, and scalar multiplication by `2` gives the left side `2x C(x)`. The right-hand `PowerSeries.mk` has coefficient `Ring.choose (1 / 2) n * (-4)^n`, exactly matching the blueprint’s definition `√(1-4x) = ∑_{n≥0} binom(1/2,n)(-4)^n x^n`. The dependency `catalan n := (2*n).choose n / (n+1)` also agrees with the Catalan-number coefficients used informally. There are no additional hypotheses or restricted binders.

The formal binders `∀ (n : ℕ), 0 < n →` match “For $n \geq 1$,” for the naturally indexed Catalan sequence. The conclusion uses `Finset.range n`, documented as the naturals less than `n`, so `∑ k ∈ Finset.range n` is exactly the sum over $k=0,\ldots,n-1$. Its summand `catalan k * catalan (n - 1 - k)` matches $c_kc_{n-1-k}$; because `k < n` and `0 < n`, natural-number subtraction does not alter the intended index. Finally, `catalan n := (2 * n).choose n / (n + 1)` represents the stated $c_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$, with `Nat.choose` supplying the binomial coefficient. No additional mathematically substantive hypothesis or narrowed summation range is introduced.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.commrin.justification: The elaborated signature quantifies exactly over a commutative ring and the stated variables: `∀ {K : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing K] (a b : K) (n : ℕ)`. Its `Finset.range (n + 1)` indexes precisely the natural numbers `k = 0, …, n`, matching `\sum_{k=0}^n`. On that range, the natural subtraction `n - k` has the intended exponent. `Nat.choose n k` is the binomial coefficient and `↑(n.choose k)` is its canonical image in `K`. The formal summand `a ^ k * b ^ (n - k) * ↑(n.choose k)` differs from the blueprint’s `\binom nk a^k b^{n-k}` only by factor order, which is immaterial under `[CommRing K]`. Thus the displayed equalities express the same binomial theorem.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.adj.justification: The two target declarations together give exactly the two parts of the blueprint’s chained equality. `mul_adjugate'` states `∀ {R} [CommRing R] {n : ℕ} (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) R), A * A.adjugate = A.det • 1`, matching `A · (adj A) = (det A) · I_n`; `adjugate_mul'` states `A.adjugate * A = A.det • 1`, matching `(adj A) · A = (det A) · I_n`. Here `Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) R` represents an `n × n` matrix, matrix `1` is the identity matrix, and scalar multiplication `A.det • 1` is determinant times that identity. The binder `[CommRing R]` matches the section’s fixed commutative ring `K`, and `{n : ℕ}` includes all natural sizes, including zero. Finally, the informal adjugate definition explicitly says that its cofactor-based definition equals Mathlib’s `Matrix.adjugate`, so using `A.adjugate` introduces no definitional drift.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.cau.justification: The blueprint fixes only “a commutative ring K” and assumes each `x_i + y_j` “is invertible in K.” The target instead quantifies over `[inst : Field K]` and assumes `h : ∀ (i j : Fin n), x i + y j ≠ 0`. In a field, nonzero is equivalent to invertible, so `h` correctly represents the denominator condition within that setting; however, `[Field K]` is a mathematically contentful added hypothesis and excludes general commutative rings having the required individual units. This restriction also enters through `cauchyMat`, whose binder is `[Field K]` and whose body uses the field inverse `(x i + y j)⁻¹`. The indexing by `Fin n` and `Finset.Ioi` faithfully represents `[n]` and `i < j`, and the displayed products otherwise match. To make the formalization faithful, generalize both `cauchy_det` and `cauchyMat` to `[CommRing K]`, replace nonzeroness by unit/invertibility witnesses for every `x i + y j`, and define the matrix entries and quotient using the corresponding inverses (or an equivalent unit-based formulation).

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.cb.justification: The blueprint quantifies over natural numbers n,m, a commutative ring K, and matrices A ∈ K^{n×m}, B ∈ K^{m×n}. This is represented by the binders `∀ {R : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing R] {n m : ℕ} (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin m) R) (B : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) R)`. The conclusion has the required `det (A * B)` and sums over `Finset.powersetCard n Finset.univ`, which, by its supplied definition, is exactly the collection of n-element subsets of the m-element index type `Fin m`, corresponding order-preservingly to subsets of `[m]`. The dependency bodies select indices in increasing order: `colsSubmatrix` is `A.submatrix id ⇑(S.orderEmbOfFin hcard)` and `rowsSubmatrix` is `B.submatrix (⇑(S.orderEmbOfFin hcard)) id`, matching the blueprint's selected columns and rows. The conditional `if h : S.card = n then ... else 0` is redundant but harmless because every `S` in `powersetCard n univ` has cardinality n; it does not alter the sum. Lean's `Matrix.det` is explicitly the Leibniz determinant, agreeing with the informal determinant definition. Thus the formal equality expresses the Cauchy–Binet formula, including the cases m<n and n=0.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.des.justification: The blueprint quantifies over “n ∈ ℕ … n ≥ 2” and an “n × n-matrix” over the commutative coefficient ring K. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.jac.justification: The target has exactly the blueprint hypotheses: `P.card = Q.card → P.card ≥ 1 →`, corresponding to `|P| = |Q| ≥ 1`, and concludes the same identity with row set `P`, column set `Q`, and complementary row/column sets `Qᶜ`, `Pᶜ`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.lap.justification: Both declarations match the two Laplace expansions. The row theorem quantifies `(p : Fin (m + 1))` and sums over `q`, while the column theorem quantifies `(q : Fin (m + 1))` and sums over `p`, exactly corresponding to “for every p” in (a) and “for every q” in (b). stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.row.justification: Every target adds the mathematically substantive binder `{K : Type u_1} [inst : CommRing K]`, whereas the blueprint only says “Let A ∈ K^{n × n}” and nowhere states that `K` is a commutative ring (or gives any other algebraic setting for `K`). stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.tra.justification: The blueprint states: “Let n ∈ ℕ. If A ∈ K^{n × n} is any n × n-matrix, then det(Aᵀ) = det A,” with K fixed as a commutative ring. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.tri.justification: Together the two declarations exactly cover the blueprint’s “triangular (i.e., lower-triangular or upper-triangular)” alternatives. The lower-triangular theorem assumes “∀ (i j : Fin n), i < j → A i j = 0” (entries above the diagonal vanish), while the upper-triangular theorem assumes “∀ (i j : Fin n), j < i → A i j = 0” (entries below the diagonal vanish). Using `Fin n` rather than the blueprint’s one-based `[n]` is only an indexing convention and does not narrow the statement.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.det.van.justification: All four declarations match the corresponding blueprint formulas. The shared binders `∀ {R : Type u_1} [CommRing R] {n : ℕ} (a : Fin n → R)` formalize “Let n ∈ ℕ” and n elements of the commutative ring K, without adding a mathematically substantive restriction. For (a), `vandermondeMat a` has entry `a i ^ (n - 1 - ↑j)`, which under 0-based `Fin n` indexing is the blueprint entry `a_i^(n-j)` under 1-based indexing; `∏ i, ∏ j ∈ Finset.Ioi i, (a i - a j)` is exactly `∏_{1 ≤ i < j ≤ n} (a_i-a_j)`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fib.bin.justification: The target quantifies exactly as the blueprint does: `∀ (n : ℕ)`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fib.gf.justification: The target is a closed equality in `PowerSeries ℚ`: the coefficient cast uses `Rat.instNatCast`, and inversion uses `PowerSeries.instInv` with `Rat.instField`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fps.1-f.justification: The formal hypothesis `∀ (n : ℕ), {i | (PowerSeries.coeff n) (f i) ≠ 0}.Finite` exactly matches “for each `n`, the set `{ i ∈ I : [x^n] f_i ≠ 0 }` is finite.” Its conclusion `PowerSeries.Multipliable fun i => 1 + f i` exactly matches “the family `(1 + f_i)_{i ∈ I}` is multipliable.” By the supplied definition, `PowerSeries.Multipliable a` means `∀ n, ∃ M, PowerSeries.DeterminesCoeffInProd a M n`, where `M : Finset I` and determination means every finite superset `J` gives the same degree-`n` coefficient as `M`; this is precisely the blueprint’s notion of finite determination of product coefficients. The binders `{R} [CommRing R] {I} {f}` supply the formal-power-series coefficient ring and arbitrary index type without adding a hypothesis beyond the mathematical setting.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-thm.fps.ant.justification: The blueprint states “For any $n\in K$” and its binomial definition explicitly allows $n$ to be “any element in a $\mathbb Q$-algebra.” The elaborated target instead quantifies over `[inst_1 : Algebra ℚ K] [inst_2 : BinomialRing K] [CharZero K]`. The `[CharZero K]` binder is an additional mathematically contentful restriction: an arbitrary commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra is not stated by the blueprint to have characteristic zero, and in particular this excludes the trivial $\mathbb Q$-algebra, while the FPS identity remains meaningful there. `BinomialRing K` can be regarded as encoding `Ring.choose` and the blueprint’s generalized binomial coefficients over a $\mathbb Q$-algebra, but `CharZero K` is not needed to state their intended meaning.
